passages.where: King Hezekiah falls ill, and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order because he will die. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays and weeps bitterly, and God answers with fifteen more years. The story is not a promise that every such prayer will be answered the same way; it is a witness that a dying person may weep and plead before God, and that God hears.

In Gethsemane Jesus falls to the ground again and again and asks the Father to take the cup from him, and in the same prayer gives his will to the Father's. The church has always read this as the prayer of one who was truly human and felt the horror of death as a real man would. Fear of dying is not a lack of faith; the Son of God prayed through it.

A man who has tried to keep silent finally prays: show me my end and the measure of my days, let me know how fleeting my life is. Every human life, he says, is only a breath. Then he asks the question that matters: what am I waiting for? My hope is in you.

Psalm 90, headed as a prayer of Moses, admits that a human life, even a long one, passes quickly and is gone. Its prayer is not for more days but for wisdom about the days: teach us to number them, so that we may gain a heart of wisdom. A short time can still be a wise time.

A man hunted by enemies and worn by grief says to God: you are my God, my times are in your hands. The psalm that holds this line also holds the words Jesus prayed on the cross, into your hands I commit my spirit. Neither the diagnosis nor the doctors hold the final measure of a believer's days.

Paul writes from prison not knowing whether he will live or die. To live is Christ and to die is gain, he says, because to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better. But he expects to stay, for the sake of the people who need him. His longing is not for death but for Christ, and he holds it together with love for those he would leave.

Facing his own execution, Paul writes to Timothy that he is already being poured out like a drink offering and the time of his departure has come. He has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith, and he looks to the crown the Lord will give. He writes it from prison, and in the same chapter asks Timothy to bring his cloak and his scrolls.

On the night before he died, Jesus tells his frightened disciples not to let their hearts be troubled, because there are many rooms in his Father's house and he goes to prepare a place for them. The site's note is careful: Jesus himself was troubled more than once, so this is not a scolding. It is a reason not to be ruled by fear, and the reason is a person and a promise: I will take you to be with me.

Standing near his friend's grave, Jesus tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies. The body's death still comes; the life he gives is not ended by it. Then he asks her, and every reader: do you believe this?

Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died, the first of a harvest still to come. He names death plainly as an enemy, the last one Christ will destroy. Scripture never asks a dying person to call death a friend.

misread.taken: The promise that the prayer offered in faith will restore the sick is sometimes used to tell a dying person, or their family, that healing would surely come if only they believed enough, so that a death is taken as a failure of faith.
misread.says: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray and to anoint them with oil, and he promises that the Lord will raise them up. Christians read the promise in more than one way, as the site's note sets out: many take it as real help that often comes as healing and is finally fulfilled in the resurrection; others stress that it depends on God's will, as Paul's unhealed thorn shows. None of these readings sets prayer against medical care, and none makes an unhealed believer guilty of too little faith. Paul prayed three times and was not healed, and no one in Scripture blames him.

whole: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone. Tell someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counselor; if you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today; and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. To be told your time is short is to have the thing everyone pushes away brought suddenly near. The fear, the grief and the disbelief that follow are not a failure of faith. There are new questions every week: treatments and their costs, what to tell the children, whether to keep working, what you still want to do, who will care for the people you leave. Some people find that the hardest part is not the dying but the waiting, and the way others stop knowing what to say.

Scripture does not pretend death is small. Paul calls it an enemy, the last one. Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept. Jesus fell to the ground in Gethsemane and asked for the cup to pass from him. These are not stories of people who failed to trust God; they are stories of people who brought their whole fear to him. The Bible also refuses to read an illness as a verdict on the person who has it. When Jesus was asked whether a man's suffering was punishment, he said no, and Paul, who prayed for relief and did not receive it, is never blamed for a lack of faith.

Wisdom in this season looks like the psalmist's prayer: teach us to number our days. Many people find it helps to ask what they want these days to hold, and to say the things that need saying while they can, words of love, of thanks, of forgiveness asked and given. It is wise to bring the practical matters into the open with the people you love and the professionals who can help, so that no one is left guessing. It is right to pray for healing, as James tells the sick to do, and right to receive good medical care; the two are not rivals. And it is right to let the church carry you: to ask the elders to pray, to let people bring meals and sit with you, to be honest with a pastor about your fear.

The Christian hope here is not a vague comfort. It is a man who walked through death ahead of us and came out the other side. Jesus told Martha he is the resurrection and the life, and he promised his frightened friends a place prepared in his Father's house. Paul, waiting for execution, could say that to depart and be with Christ is far better, and still choose to stay as long as he was needed. Your times are in God's hands, not only in the hands of the doctors. Death is still an enemy, and it still costs everything. But for those who belong to Christ it is not the end of the story, and it is not the last word about you.
sit: If your days are fewer than you hoped, what is one thing you most want to say, and to whom?

prayer.lead: The opening of Psalm 31 ends with the words Jesus prayed on the cross. Pray them as your own, and let the last line be a trust you are still learning.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
Seeking help is not a failure of faith.
